Combing through SMB Bench traces this week, looking for emergent model capabilities, reminded me of my first intro to AI course in undergrad.

Our term project was a class competition to build the best Poker Solitaire bot (Poker Squares: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poker_squares). You draw 25 cards one at a time, place them permanently on a 5x5 grid, and score all 5 rows and 5 columns as poker hands. I was particularly interested in the problem and was convinced I could get first place in the class.

I spent days doing manual research, looking at papers, similar games/competitions, and running ablations to squeeze every point out of a Java bot with 30 seconds per game.

Today I dug up that code and asked a frontier model to beat it. Instead of days hunting for what an expert would try. In about 60 seconds, it built a version that scores nearly 10% higher than my best working bot, while running 40x faster (0.73s vs 30s).

In the competition, some classmates went for Hail Marys, chasing rare hands for one massive game that rarely materialised. The real game was choosing the move with the highest expected value for that situation. That same dynamic plays out with LLMs today. You often see emergent behaviour where a model nails something once on a lucky roll, but post-training is what elicits that behaviour consistently enough to actually push the frontier.

Intro AI courses and the research definitely look different now, yet the methodology feels the same: go deep, inspect outputs, and hunt for the next experiment that unlocks better performance.

For anyone curious, here are the versions I still have code for (I ran 100 seeds to get average scores):

Random & Flush baselines (7.9 / 23.9 avg): Starter bots using random placement and simple suit-stacking.

Symmetry sketch (MCPlayer): Early draft rotating the grid before realizing empty rows/cols are interchangeable, so a bounding box plus one empty row/col is enough. I remember such a 💡 moment when I figured out that checking the expected value of some moves was redundant because they were equivalent.

Random-rollout Upper Confidence Bound (RandomMultiUCBMCPlayer, 43.4 avg): Multi-threaded UCB1 search, symmetry pruning, empirically profiled 30s time budget, random playouts. This was a big level-up for knowledge and strategy

Greedy-rollout UCB (OptimizedMultiUCBMCPlayer, 50.7 avg): Depth-12 greedy rollouts with incremental row/col delta scoring. My best working submission. So much fiddling and iterations with this one, different depths, calibrating thresholds, and reading outputs after each run to tweak and run again for an hour.

Bit-twiddling evaluator (CustomMCPlayer, 50.7 avg): Ported a 10-line bit-manipulation hand scorer that broke even since it only ran on full 5-card hands.

Cached row/col scoring (MoreOptimizedMultiUCBMCPlayer, 16.7 avg): Cached row and column scores for faster rollouts, but accidentally swapped the two arrays. I was right up against the deadline with no time to debug why it tanked. Fixing that bug today bumps it to 53.0 avg.

Feeling nostalgic for what learning and this work used to look like, but incredibly excited that I get to apply the same methodology to problems that I wouldn't have even dreamed possible back then.

v Video courtesy of the same model that mogged me with its modern RL player that takes < 1s to beat all my attempts.

This is one of the strangest computers ever built.

It runs on about 200,000 living human brain cells grown on a chip, and those cells taught themselves to play Doom.

It's called the CL1, an Australian startup called Cortical Labs sells it for $35,000, and they're already stacking them into server racks.

How you teach a dish of neurons to play a video game is the wild part:

> The cells sit on a grid of electrodes that can both zap them and listen to them.

> The game gets turned into electrical pulses, so the cells "feel" where the enemies are, and their own firing gets read back as moves.

> When they play well, they get a calm, predictable signal. When they mess up, they get blasted with random noise.

> Brain cells seem to hate unpredictability, so they slowly rewire themselves to get more of the calm signal. That's the learning.

Teaching an earlier version Pong took the team 18 months. Doom took under a week.

They still play like a total beginner, by the team's own account, and right now they're mostly sold for testing drugs on real human neurons.

But a computer that's alive and learns on its own, at about 30 watts a unit, was pure science fiction a few years ago.

Getting A to bind B is no longer the most significant challenge. RFD4, BindCraft2, and mol-1 all shipped during the @adaptyv  x @AnthropicAI  binder competition.

The real challenge is everything required for an actual therapeutic: cross-species binding (human + mouse), pH-gated switching, receptor agonism, and mutant vs wild-type selectivity.

Those constraints require real reasoning beyond SOTA models. So Proteus Bio x @FinalDoseLFG  tested where that intelligence and intuition should live: human or AI?

We ran three distinct architectures across the competition:

Route A: The Orchestrator (LLM driving SOTA tools). An LLM agent orchestrating BindCraft2 and ESMdesign. It worked early on, filtering nicely for pH selectivity, until it hit hard targets like TNF. Our agent generated binders that folded with high confidence but refused to co-fold on both human and mouse. It burned cycles spamming new seeds and hotspots until progress flatlined.
Route B: The Craftsman (Human expert driving SOTA tools). Tarun JaiRaj Narwani, FinalDose’s seasoned protein designer, ran the same stack. On GLP-1R, Route A kept falling into the extracellular groove "affinity trap," churning out potent antagonists. Tarun bypassed it with mechanistic restraints, engineering a 30 Å de novo "helical lance" straight into the transmembrane core to salt-bridge Arg190 and engage Gln234. That repacked the central polar network, displaced the pocket floor, and unlatched the conserved TM6 proline kink to swing the helix into the active Gαs register (counter-screened against inactive 6LN2 co-folds). The only bottleneck was time. With new targets dropping every 1–2 weeks alongside his full-time role at FinalDose, expert human attention was our scarcest resource.

Route C: The Alchemist (LLM designing the molecule directly). This is our bread and butter at Proteus Bio. We built an agent harness where the LLM doesn't touch RFD4, BC2, or ESMdesign, and there is no inverse folding. It writes and mutates the raw amino acid sequence itself through hypothesis-driven evolution: "Put a Threonine here to cap that helix. "Mutate this to Histidine and refold." A co-folding model scores each proposal in seconds to minutes, letting the agent discard bad hypotheses almost as fast as it writes them while respecting target constraints. Within 30 iterations, it was beating the SOTA tools.

As @sklin_lite said:  "Watching an LLM with zero design tools out-evolve SOTA pipelines in 30 loops with no breaks and zero attention scarcity convinced me this is the next generation of drug design."

So, whose intelligence wins? It depends where you put it:→ Put AI on top of design tools, and it plateaus when the tools do.→ Put a human expert on the tools, and they thrive until they run out of hours.→ Put human intelligence into the harness and AI intelligence directly into the sequence with fast feedback, and it compounds tirelessly.

What a run.
P.S. Massive shoutout to @Tenstorrent (@moritzthuening) for the blazing-fast compute powering all that refolding.
